speechtext: [English)

Mr. Speaker, the protection of the environment was given a boost at the conference of the Interparliamentary Union held in Guatemala last week when parliamentarians from over 100 nations adopted a strongly worded document on environmental protection and sustainable development.
The policy document which is now being reported to other Parliaments as well contains substantial recommendations on key subjects such as the protection of the ozone layer, energy efficiency, pollution control, acid rain abatement, conservation of natural resources, population policies, debt relief to developing countries, climate protection, genetic diversity, development assistance, peace, arms race and disarmament, transportation of toxic wastes, education, protection of the world's artistic and cultural heritage, tropical forests and the like.
Parliamentarians have an important role in informing the public about global trends which affect our life on this planet. This policy document which is now available should be the object of serious consideration by all parliamentarians here in Ottawa and by the Government of Canada.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-SUPPORT FROM CANADIAN REAL ESTATE ASSOCIATION
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-SUPPORT FROM CANADIAN REAL ESTATE ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 70,000 Canadians cannot be all wrong. The Canadian Real Estate Association, CREA, which is holding its annual executive meeting here in Ottawa, has given its full support to the free trade agreement with the United States. They as well as a growing number of Canadians realize the benefits that the
free trade agreement will bring to the service industry in Canada.
Homes in Canada will cost less to purchase. Opportunities and growth will occur in all related industries. This alone will translate into a great many jobs across Canada. As a service industry, the Canadian Real Estate Association understands the importance of such an agreement. We must ensure our existing markets and create more.
The service industry is one of the fastest growing Canadian exports. In coming years Canada must be ready to accept the challenge and offer our children the chance to grow and live in their native land.
CREA, like a great many other national associations, is encouraging the acceptance of the free trade agreement with the U.S. as a great step forward in maintaining our freedom and expanding our economic base. For CREA and all Canadians let us make sure we take advantage of this great opportunity.

subsubtopic: SUPERMAILBOXES-DISADVANTAGES TO USE BY ELDERLY AND THE DISABLED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister responsible for the Post Office declared to a group of citizens soon after his appointment that he was not responsible for the Post Office. Perhaps this explains why he has refused to take decisive corrective action on issues of such fundamental importance to many Canadians as that of supermailboxes.
The supermailbox program disadvantages the elderly and disabled, making the mail virtually inaccessible during the rigours of winter. Supermailboxes have adversely affected property values and there are serious security concerns associated with them.
Instead of recognizing that supermailboxes were a super grandiose disaster and revoking the policy, the Minister chooses to fudge the numbers and tells Canadians that to extend home mail delivery to all homes would cause the price of a first-class stamp to rise to 60 cents. That is utter nonsense and he knows it.

April 20, 1988
In response to a question I put to him in the House on this topic he said that in front of his house there was a mailbox, an electrical utility box, and telephone poles. That later proved to be incorrect. Clearly the Minister is not responsible to the Canadian public. Clearly it is time he offered his resignation.

Mr. Speaker, the Government must be congratulated on taking a difficult but correct decision in deporting bogus refugees such as the Turks. This decision means personal hardship for those individuals. However, it is imperative that the world be given this clear, concise message: liars and cheaters are not welcome in Canada.
Genuine refugees are welcome. Immigrants who have waited in the immigration process are welcome. However, fairness dictates queue jumpers are not welcome.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER OF JUSTICE AMEND LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise again today to bring up once more the problem of family violence. I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) several times to reflect on this deplorable situation of family violence in this country. We have learned that, following Ontario's lead, Quebec's Minister of Justice yesterday increased his budget by $1.8 million to deal with the growing number of cases of family violence.
Yesterday morning, before the parliamentary committee reviewing his Estimates, the Minister of Justice said that the number of attorneys dealing with such cases increased fivefold in 1987 alone. Also, the various police forces in Quebec had to answer 6,559 cases involving offences. New services were set up, such as telephone services to help the victims of family violence.
That is not enough. Mr. Speaker, we must still re-examine the cause of this violence as well as amend the law. One of the things that could be done is, instead of taking women and children from their homes and sending them to shelters, to send the spouses and husbands who are responsible for this violence to shelters. The federal Government has cut grants, with the result that the shelters are not big enough and are now overcrowded.
So I again ask the Minister of Justice to reconsider bringing in amendments to improve the present law in cases of family violence.

Mr. Speaker, last week our colleague, the Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean), and I had the opportunity and privilege of attending the World Conference on Global Survival held at Christ Church, Oxford University, England.
It was organized jointly by the Global Committee of Parliamentarians on Population and Development together with the Temple of Understanding, and served to bring together for the first time over 100 spiritual leaders of the major world religions with a like number of parliamentarians from around the world to talk about issues which challenge the very survival of life on our planet.
This unique conference heard keynote speakers in the arts and sciences who had messages to offer to the delegates. Workshops of smaller numbers provided excellent opportunities for sharing and exchanging views on three main topics, namely, physical and spiritual resources, crisis and human responsibility, and global opportunities.
The conference concluded by approving a statement which I shall circulate in both official languages to all Members of this House and the other place.

Mr. Speaker, the Canada Post Corporation is trying to sell its privatization policy by telling small businesses they can't lose on a postal concession because it will attract more customers.
However, privatization has the effect of dramatically reducing the salaries of employees who work in those concessions, and we know that most of these employees are women. This policy will certainly not help reduce the wage gap between men and women.
April 20, 1988



As well, Mr. Speaker, Canada Post is giving its services an image that is certainly inappropriate for a government corporation. Many of these new franchises are convenience stores or video rentals that are selling pornography. Many women, and certainly those with children, are not interested in having to patronize stores that sell images that are degrading to women and disturbing to children.
The Government, in supporting Canada Post's policy of privatization, has clearly shown once again its lack of commitment to equality for Canadian women and to the strength of Canadian families.

Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome this opportunity to draw the attention of the House to the cordial and supportive reception members of the select Club de la garnison de Quebec gave on April 18 to Canada's Minister of National Defence, the Hon. Perrin Beatty.
For those attending, it was a unique opportunity to become more familiar with the Conservative Government's defence policy.
In keeping with its respect for the democratic process, the Mulroney Government has proceeded with many consultations on the views of Canadians about "peace and order in Canada". The concerns expressed in the course of these consultations will help us determine how we can make Canada a country that seeks peace through freedom, and security through international cooperation.
Mr. Speaker, the present Government will continue to meet its responsibility, which is that of any free and sovereign State, to ensure our common freedom and security.

Mr. Speaker, this morning, the federal Liberal Caucus met the President of the Association culturelle franco-canadienne de la Saskatchewan. Rupert Baudais, a Saskatchewan Francophone from Prince Albert whose ancestors settled in Saskatchewan in 1883, was accompanied by Vice President Margot Michaud of Gravel-bourg and the proud President of Jeunesse fransaskoise, Francis Machildon of Zenon Park, where I had the privilege of campaigning several times back in 1964 and 1967.
Oral Questions
They expressed their anxiety and concern, now that the Conservative Government in Saskatchewan, under the leadership of Mr. Devine, is about to adopt Bill 2. I hope Mr. Devine's government will review its position and start by consulting with those directly concerned, the Saskatchewan Francophones themselves. I found their representations so reasonable, and I wish they were better known to Canadians, that I fail to see why the government intends to adopt this Bill. The Fransaskois are reasonable people. They are asking far less than what is already provided by Section 133 of the Constitution in Quebec to protect our Anglophone minority, and I hope that.. .
Altogether, we should depoliticize this question and ask Mr. Devine to take the necessary steps by consulting the fransaskois themselves.

subsubtopic: ARTICLE PUBLISHED IN LE MONDE JURIDIQUE-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. For nearly two weeks now, the Prime Minister's Office has been aware that Le Monde juridique was to publish an important article on Judge Crete's succession. I therefore ask the Minister of Justice: When the Prime Minister's Office was informed on April 5, was the Minister of Justice also informed that the article was to be published?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ARTICLE PUBLISHED IN LE MONDE JURIDIQUE-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must tell the Hon. Member that this matter was brought to my attention in a very general way possibly within the last two weeks, but it had not been published and there had been an absolute denial.
I think the Hon. Member will know that, indeed, Mr. Yves Pratte wrote to the publisher and the author of this article, indicating that it was without foundation and there would be serious legal consequences if the publication proceeded.
As we now discuss this matter, legal proceedings are being initiated to have this matter dealt with by a court of law. According to my information, I understand there will be an action commenced and served within the next day against the author, against the publisher and other defendants with respect to this matter. An absolute denial by Mr. Roy has been made public. I hope the Hon. Member will accept the statement at this time and let the court decide exactly what are the circumstances.

April 20, 1988
Oral Questions

subtopic: INDEPENDENCE OF JUSTICE-REQUEST THAT MINISTER INSTITUTE INQUIRY
INDEPENDENCE OF JUSTICE-REQUEST THAT MINISTER INSTITUTE INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask a supplementary question, because yesterday evening again, Mr. Andre Gagnon, who is a law graduate, was attached to Quebec's Minister of Justice and is editor in chief of this specialized journal, continued to maintain his allegations. Therefore I ask the Minister of Justice, setting aside the civil matter involving Bernard Roy, does he not think that it is his duty as Minister of Justice to look after the public interest and to ensure the independence of justice? Given the seriousness of the allegations, has he considered instituting an inquiry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INDEPENDENCE OF JUSTICE-REQUEST THAT MINISTER INSTITUTE INQUIRY
speechtext:

Member that at no time has there been any influence attempted by any member of the Cabinet with respect to judicial appointments. subtopic: REQUEST THAT MATTER BE REFERRED TO COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND SOLICITOR GENERAL
REQUEST THAT MATTER BE REFERRED TO COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Justice. Outside the civil and private matter involving Mr. Roy, would it not be in the interest of this House and of justice for this matter to be referred to the Committee on Justice and Solicitor General, where Mr. Gagnon himself has told us he is ready to testify at any time because he knows that civil proceedings could take very long and that we would be in doubt for a long time? Hopefully, in the interest of Mr. Roy as well, this will be cleared up as soon as possible. Could the Minister of Justice suggest some procedure like that where the integrity of the process would no longer be at stake?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MATTER BE REFERRED TO COMMITTEE ON JUSTICE AND SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course we can have any number of proceedings at the same time. I believe the Hon. Member is a lawyer who has standing at the Bar of Quebec. I think he will understand that when a very serious allegation is made with respect to the integrity of an individual, that person, regardless of their position in our country, is entitled to seek legal recourse. I think that is what Mr. Roy intends to do and
is in the process of doing. I think the matter will be dealt with expeditiously, that justice will be served in the courts, and that the full story will come out.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Public Works. It concerns the latest scandalous misuse of taxpayers' dollars by the Canada Lands Company at Mirabel. Can the Minister explain to the House why the Canada Lands Company at Mirabel spent $61,000 of taxpayers' money to publish five thousand 24-page colour brochures featuring the Member of Parliament for Joliette (Mr. LaSalle) and his cousin Pierre Hardy congratulating each other for the fine mess they created at Mirabel? Is this Pierre Hardy's revenge, or is this Roch LaSalle's last hurrah?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stewart Mclnnes (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the previous Government expropriated 98,000 acres of property which adversely affected some 10,000 people. It spent $225 million and engaged in $100 million worth of law suits. This Government settled the law suits, brought in investment to the extent of $22 million, restored the properties, and social justice has now been given to the people. It is a good investment to tell that story.
I don't blame the Minister for not answering the question. He is probably just as embarrassed over this as everyone else.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works to explain to the House why a contract for $36,960 was awarded to have this publication printed and why the contract was split in two, which contravenes Chapter 310 of the Administrative Policy Manual.
Why did this happen? Why were Treasury Board guidelines ignored?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stewart Mclnnes (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would think an expenditure of $1 million would not be enough to remind the people of Canada of the mismanagement and scandal of that Government.

April 20, 1988

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-TREATMENT OF FOREIGN FIRMS IN CANADA
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-TREATMENT OF FOREIGN FIRMS IN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade. Last night The Journal ran a powerful documentary-

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-TREATMENT OF FOREIGN FIRMS IN CANADA
speechtext: -on the losses in economic independence that this country will suffer from the U.S. trade deal. That is the true tragedy of this deal. Will the Minister be forthright and confirm one of the key points made in that documentary, that this deal would prevent us from ever putting in place performance requirements on a foreign firm such as those we put on RCA, which gave us Spar Aerospace, now a dynamic high-tech firm with exports world-wide?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-TREATMENT OF FOREIGN FIRMS IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, luckily last night I was able to watch this program which the hon. gentleman describes as powerful. I found the arguments put forward by Mr. Lipsey to be most powerful, convincing, and intellectually honest. I don't want to mention any of the politicians who were on the program, but the Minister of Finance was a shining star there as well.
The U.S. Canada Free Trade Agreement does not in any way prevent us from acting. It governs how we may act in certain situations but it certainly does not prevent us from acting.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-TREATMENT OF FOREIGN FIRMS IN CANADA
speechtext: You are acting now.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-TREATMENT OF FOREIGN FIRMS IN CANADA
speechtext: We have to act in ways that are fair and nondiscriminatory with the people who engage with our chief trading partner, just as they have to treat us fairly in a nondiscriminatory way down there. That is the nature of the bargain. That is a very powerful case for approval of this agreement, as soon as we can get it, so that regime will commence.

Mr. Speaker, since the Minister claims that this is a non-discriminatory deal let me ask him this question. Is it not true that if a foreign company from another country is involved then performance requirements are possible, but if a company from the United States is involved then performance requirements are not possible? In short, there is complete discrimination here. Are these not the facts?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course those are not the facts. I have not
Oral Questions
heard the Hon. Member give a fact yet in this whole discussion.
As far as whether it is discriminatory or not, let us look to an outside source, Mr. Arthur Dunkel, the GATT Secretary-General, who said this as quoted in today's Globe and Mail.
The proposed free-trade pact between Canada and the United States "will
in no way hinder" each country's trading obligations with the rest of the
world-
He is advised by his Secretariat that the agreement generally conforms with the crucial section of the GATT charter banning discriminatory trade practices against other nations.
That is the hallmark of this agreement. What is sauce for the goose in the agreement is sauce for the gander.

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly clear who got goosed in this particular agreement. I have to say that it is definitely this country.
I want to suggest a last question to the Minister since he listened only to one side of the argument last night. It was the argument of those in favour of the deal, such as Mr. D'Aquino, who was absolutely clear that there was some loss of independence. How can he justify this giving away of Canadian independence for no more than jobs 25,000 per year, which is the maximum estimation of the Economic Council of Canada? How can he justify that?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what the hon. gentleman forgets is that what is good for the Oshawa goose should be good for the Canadian gander generally.
Hear, hear!

There is no loss of independence under this agreement. There is a loss in certain choices that can be made, just as when we entered into the GATT agreement. The hon. gentleman's Party believes in GATT. Why was it not up moaning and shrieking about GATT when we entered into the GATT?
There is a certain loss of independence in the sense that one loses certain choices because it is a bargain between two independent countries. When a man and a woman marry they each give up certain of their independence. Would anybody say that they are both slaves? They might be love slaves, but they are not slaves in any other direction.
Oh, oh!

The hon. gentleman's argument is completely silly. The Americans give up certain rights of independent action of theirs in certain areas, as do we, for our mutual benefit, for increasing the economic wealth of the two countries. For heaven's sake, grasp the fundamentals.

April 20, 1988
Oral Questions FINANCE

subtopic: FLOW-THROUGH SHARES TAX DEDUCTION-EFFECT ON MINERAL EXPLORATION
FLOW-THROUGH SHARES TAX DEDUCTION-EFFECT ON MINERAL EXPLORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. On March 1 of this year John Larche, President of the Prospectors & Developers Association of Canada, said that flow-throughs can perform despite the market conditions. He went on to say that at present flow-through is the only viable means of raising risk capital for mineral exploration.
On Monday of this week the Minister of National Revenue said in reply to a question I raised on flow-through shares: " ... the Government is giving the matter close consideration."
I wish to ask the Minister of Finance this. When will he be ready to act? When will he give a favourable announcement and tell the mineral industry that this first-rate excellent tool for economic development is going to be retained?

subtopic: FLOW-THROUGH SHARES TAX DEDUCTION-EFFECT ON MINERAL EXPLORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me reaffirm what my colleague said on Monday. We are giving close consideration to this particular matter. Let me also say to the Member posing the question that the flowthrough share mechanism has been retained.
There are some allegations made that tax reform has had some serious effects on the flow-through share mechanism. I would point out to the Hon. Member, as I have on previous occasions in the House, that the change since the stock market crash of October 19 has had the effect of upsetting equity financing for all industries, not only flow-through shares.
These are things that have come to bear on the attractiveness of flow-through share financing to investors. We are considering this matter closely, and in a short time I hope that I will have some announcements.

Mr. Speaker, that, of course, comes as good news. I wish to remind the Minister that he knows the industry does not want grants or subsidies. What it wants is retention of the earned depletion allowance. Time is a vital factor, because there are projects that are presently on hold, and also jobs.
I want to say to the Minister, if he is reluctant to accept these demands from the Opposition that, if he would listen to some of his own Members from the ridings of Timmins- Chapleau, Timiskaming, Western Arctic, and Abitibi, he will get exactly the same response, and that is, save the flowthrough.

Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated, we are fully in agreement. We are saving the flow-through share.
We made some changes in the December announcements on tax reform which changed some of the provisions of the flowthrough share financing with a view to improving its attractiveness.
The Hon. Member says that we should extend earned depletions. I also ask him to consider what he and others of his Party have said, that we should avoid tax shelter gimmicks. The Hon. Member is shaking is head.
Not gimmicks.

The Hon. Member should read some of the literature that his Party has written, and some of the things that his colleagues have said. This is one of the considerations that we are going through in discussions that we are having on flow-through share financing. I would expect that we would get his support.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister about language rights in Saskatchewan. Yesterday, the Prime Minister said he was pleased with Premier Devine's intention to declare Saskatchewan bilingual fifteen years from now, but strangely enough, he refused to criticize Bill 2 which will deny the historical and age-old rights of the Francophone minority in Saskatchewan. My question is this: Since the federal Government and the provincial Government are negotiating the future of the Fransaskois in their absence and in the upmost secrecy, is the Government now prepared to make a commitment to involve representatives of the Francophone minority of Saskatchewan directly in these negotiations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the interest of the New Democratic Party in this issue with respect to the Province of Saskatchewan. In fact, the federal Government, through my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and I believe through other officials of government who are dealing with this particular issue, is in communication with L'Association des fransaskois. 1 think that I have made it a point to keep them fully informed with respect to the position of the federal Government in this matter.
As far as I am aware, there have also been communications with the French minority group in Saskatchewan by the provincial Government. It is in the process of ongoing discussions with them, and receiving the benefit of their views.
As I indicated, and as the Prime Minister has indicated, it is our hope that we will be able in our discussions-and I like to
April 20, 1988

term them as discussions as opposed to negotiations-to make our position quite clear. The Prime Minister has stated in the House of Commons, outside the House of Commons, and in a letter to Premier Devine, the position which we as a federal Government take.
On these issues at this point in time, we are always wanting to carry on these discussions to resolve them on a co-operative basis. That is my hope for Saskatchewan. I trust that the members of the New Democratic Party share that particular point of view.

Mr. Speaker, is the Minister of Justice not aware that L'Association des fransas-kois, which has taken the trouble to come here to meet with the three caucuses over the last 24 hours, has stated quite specifically that it is excluded from participating in, from being present, or involved in any way in the negotiations or discussions that are now under way between the federal Government and the provincial Government?
In the meantime, Premier Devine refuses either to abandon or withdraw Bill 2, or substantially amend it.
Under those circumstances, is the Government ready now to come to the aid of the proposal of my Leader that the three political Parties in this Chamber should come together with a resolution which would clearly signal the desire of every Member of Parliament to support the rights of the francophone minority in Saskatchewan, and press the Government of that province to delay adopting Bill 2 until there has been a real consultation with the Saskatchewan francophone minority?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I find it strange that the Hon. Member put the question in the manner that he did. If he talked to his colleagues in the New Democratic caucus who come from the Province of Saskatchewan, he might be able to understand the nature of this problem.
We do.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is a problem which resulted from the Supreme Court decision, which is a matter within the provincial domain and jurisdiction at the present time. We in the federal Government have taken exemplary leadership in going forward and trying to assist the Province of Saskatchewan as best we can in the interests of the minority in Saskatchewan to resolve this matter.
Am I to take it that the Hon. Member is stating the position of the New Democratic Party, the federal New Democratic Party and, indeed, the provincial New Democratic Party, that he does not want us to carry on with these discussions to advance the cause of minority rights in Saskatchewan? Is that the position the Hon. Member is taking? If that is the case, shame on him.
Oral Questions
We want the fransaskois to be involved.

subsubtopic: FRENCH FACT IN QUEBEC-PUBLIC SERVICE LANGUAGE TEACHERS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. It concerns his Government's attitude in two cases: First, the transfer of funds from the Department of the Secretary of State to Alliance Quebec, funds that are used to fight the French fact in Quebec and Bill 101; second, the Government's cavalier treatment of Public Service language teachers with respect to their working conditions and the impact this will have on the availability of services in French to all Canadians.
My question is this: Is the Deputy Prime Minister aware of the fact that Alliance Quebec obtained $1,109,000 in 1984; $1,183,000 in 1985; $1,150,000 in 1986; and $1,215,0000 in 1987? And this is still going on now! Is he aware of the fact that these funds have been used largely to fight the French fact and Bill 101 in Quebec? What do the Deputy Prime Minister and his Government intend to do to remedy a situation that is both unfair and dangerous?

subsubtopic: FRENCH FACT IN QUEBEC-PUBLIC SERVICE LANGUAGE TEACHERS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the direction in which the Hon. Member is pointing his question is a perilous one, because I think it would be extremely imprudent to make any value judgments about the way Alliance Quebec's funds are spent. I was once Secretary of State and I was involved in providing assistance to all language minorities in this country, both in Quebec and outside that province, to both Anglophone and Francophone minorities. I think the policies of the Department of the Secretary of State, which were established before this Government and which consist in helping minorities, are excellent and should be maintained as a reflection of the way this country was built and the way we want to continue to live in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I have the facts here and I can show the Minister.
Now, about our language teachers: What do the Deputy Prime Minister and his Government intend to do about their working conditions, since these will have a direct negative impact on French services offered to Canadians across this country, and also considering the fact that his Government's attitude seems to be in direct contradiction with the Government's own language policies?

April 20, 1988
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of State and Minister of State (Treasury Board)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, questions have been asked about that particular strike several times in the House.
We have indicated that the Government accepts the majority report of the conciliation board and that it is ready to go back to the bargaining table with the language teachers at any time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to come back to the Saskatchewan question and ask the Minister of Justice a question. Yesterday in the House the Prime Minister, in answer to a question I put to him, said:
In rny judgment, and I believe in the view of my hon. friend, minority rights
are indivisible. You either believe in the protection of minority rights or you do
not. You do not believe in them three-quarters of the time or half the time.
That is the position that I adopted in Saskatchewan-
That was the position of the Prime Minister yesterday. We know that there are existing acquired rights in Saskatchewan now in regard to languages, French and English. We know that Section 110 of the Northwest Territories Act gave that obligation and gave that access to the people of Saskatchewan in both English and French. There exist today certain rights.
Does the Minister believe that the Government of Saskatchewan in proposing to abrogate those rights, to reduce those rights, to make them possibly subject to the whims of Governments, is meeting the requirements of the Prime Minister, that the rights are indivisible, that you believe in them fully, that you do not cut them up and do not abrogate them?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course I stand with and behind the Prime Minister in his position with respect to the indivisibility of minority rights in our country. That is why the Prime Minister has taken so many initiatives with respect to this issue in the time that he has been Leader of our Party in opposition and in government as Prime Minister.
1 think the Hon. Member would agree with me that the Supreme Court itself in its judgment recognizes the fact that its declaration with respect to this issue was one which indicated that there should not be a declaration at the time of the judgment and that there should be a reasonable opportunity for appropriate measures to be put into place with respect to the rights of the minority.
What I am saying is that it is important for us on an urgent basis to do what we can in the federal regime to assist the Province of Saskatchewan to meet the full implications of the Mercure decision of the Supreme Court of Canada. In that I share the same point of view as the Hon. Member. There is no difference between us. It is a question of us working has hard as possible to obtain justice for minority rights in Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister is condemning Premier Devine who is actually going to abrogate those rights. If I understand the Minister clearly, he is actually critical of the measure before the Saskatchewan Government, because the Minister cannot have it both ways. You must either stand or not stand. That problem is there. You cannot have it half way.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Fransaskois who were here today told us they were not involved in current talks between the federal Government and Saskatchewan. Oral Questions TAX REFORM

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Last week the Government released draft legislation on taxation in 360 pages of arcane language, with no index or table of contents, and no technical notes. The public is given only until May 20 to respond.
Is this the Minister's idea of appropriate consultation on a major tax change?

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is well aware that we heard the first reports of this as a result of tax reform in December and we have had a fair amount of consultation with the community since that time. In fact, there has been quite a bit of consultation. I do not think that there are any new concepts in the proposals released last week. I think that that, together with the ongoing process of legislative review, which will probably take us into June when we get to the final legislation, will give plenty of opportunity for people to provide us with their views.

subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF SECOND PHASE OF TAX REFORM
INTRODUCTION OF SECOND PHASE OF TAX REFORM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister set the date of May 20, and much of this is in fact new. The Minister also continues to put off introduction of phase two of tax reform, although he calls the present sales tax system a silent killer of jobs. Why does he want to rush through phase one without proper examination while phase two remains shrouded in mystery until after the next election?

subtopic: INTRODUCTION OF SECOND PHASE OF TAX REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me be quite clear. The comments we are looking for by May 20 are on the draft legislation. There will be final legislation put forward then. That can be amended, as my hon. friend is well aware, so I do not want to have her leave the impression that May 20 is the last opportunity.
As regards phase two, my colleague is quite aware of the very full discussions we are having with the provinces and others. There is a difference between phase one and phase two. Phase one involves a number of changes to the existing system. Phase two involves the introduction of a new sales tax system. That is why we must have these fuller discussions. There are some very complex issues at stake.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for his question, and I share his concerns and the concerns of all Canadians and the Canadian Government about the situation facing millions of Ethiopians today.
Last week, the Hon. Member raised the question of the delivery of aid by non-governmental organizations.
Mr. Speaker, the NGOs play a very important role in the delivery of our aid programs in Ethiopia and elsewhere, but today, when we consider the possibility of delivery through Sudan, the point is that we are not sure, and we are now trying to find out, whether the Sudanese port and the various routes would be able to handle and carry this aid to the people who need it.
We are concerned about finding the best way to route this aid, and we believe that if the Government allows NGOs to return to the North, that would be the best solution to the problem of how to deliver aid to the people that need it.
